title: Select, use and care for engineering power tools

lessons.title: Types of power tools and choosing the right one
lessons.html:
Power tools in the workshop

Power tools make work faster, but they can also cause serious injuries in a moment. Choosing the right tool for the job is the first step to working safely.

Common engineering power tools

ToolUse
Electric drillDrilling holes in metal, wood or plastic
Pedestal (pillar) drillAccurate, straight holes; work clamped in a vice
Angle grinderCutting, grinding welds, removing rust with discs or wire wheels
Bench grinderSharpening tools, shaping small parts
Impact wrench (electric or air)Loosening and tightening wheel nuts and large bolts
Air ratchetFast removal of nuts in tight spaces
Jigsaw / reciprocating sawCutting sheet metal, pipes and profiles
Cut-off sawStraight cuts on steel bar, tube and angle iron

Power sources

  • Electric (mains): 230 V tools with a cable. Risk of shock if cables are damaged or wet.
  • Battery (cordless): no cable to trip on, good for field repairs.
  • Pneumatic (air): powered by a compressor; no shock risk but air hoses and pressure must be managed.

Selecting the tool

  • Match the tool to the job and material.
  • Choose the correct accessory: drill bit for metal, cutting disc or grinding disc.
  • Check that the disc or wheel is rated for the tool's speed (rpm). Never fit a disc rated lower than the tool speed.
  • Use the correct size: a small grinder for light work, a bigger one for heavy work.
  • Never use a tool for a job it was not designed for, such as using a grinder as a saw for wood without the correct guard and blade.

lessons.title: Using power tools safely
lessons.html:
Before you start

  • Only use tools you have been trained and authorised to use.
  • Inspect the tool: cable and plug undamaged, switch working, guard fitted, handle secure, no cracks.
  • Inspect accessories: no cracked discs, blunt bits or missing teeth.
  • Check air hoses and couplings on pneumatic tools.
  • Use an earth leakage-protected outlet for electric tools.
  • Clear the work area of flammables, especially when grinding.

Personal protective equipment

  • Safety glasses or a face shield (face shield for grinding)
  • Hearing protection
  • Gloves suited to the task, but not loose gloves near rotating drills where they can be caught
  • Dust mask when grinding or cutting
  • Close-fitting clothing; tie back long hair and remove jewellery

Safe operation

  1. Clamp the work securely in a vice or with clamps. Never hold small parts by hand while drilling.
  2. Hold the tool firmly with both hands where designed.
  3. Stand balanced and keep your body out of the line of the disc or bit.
  4. Let the tool reach full speed before touching the work.
  5. Do not force the tool; let it do the work.
  6. Keep the cable or hose away from the cutting area.
  7. Switch off and wait for it to stop completely before putting it down.

Specific dangers

  • Angle grinder kickback: if the disc jams, the grinder can jump violently. Keep the guard in place and use the side handle.
  • Drill grab: when breaking through metal, the drill can grab and spin the work. Clamp the work and ease pressure at breakthrough.
  • Bench grinder: keep the tool rest close to the wheel, with only a small gap as set by the maker, so work cannot be pulled in.
  • Compressed air: never point at a person or use it to blow dust off your body.

Disconnect power before changing discs, bits or blades.

lessons.title: Caring for and storing power tools
lessons.html:
Keeping tools in good condition

After use

  • Switch off and unplug, remove the battery, or disconnect the air supply.
  • Let the tool cool.
  • Clean off dust, swarf and grease with a brush or cloth. Do not use compressed air to clean electric tools if the maker advises against it, as it can push dust into the motor.
  • Check for damage and wear.
  • Coil cables loosely; do not wrap tightly around the tool.

Routine maintenance

  • Keep ventilation slots clear so the motor does not overheat.
  • Oil pneumatic tools as the maker recommends, usually a few drops in the air inlet daily, unless they are oil-free types.
  • Drain water from the compressor tank and air lines regularly.
  • Replace worn carbon brushes, chuck keys and side handles when needed, using the maker's parts.
  • Have electric tools inspected and tested at the intervals set by your workplace.

Accessories

  • Store drill bits in an index box by size.
  • Keep discs flat and dry; damp or dropped discs can crack.
  • Throw away discs that are worn to the minimum size, cracked or past their expiry date.
  • Sharpen or replace blunt drill bits.

Storage

  • Store tools in their cases or on marked shelves.
  • Keep them in a dry, secure place.
  • Keep batteries charged as the maker advises and away from heat.
  • Use a tool register so you know who has which tool.

Faulty tools

If a tool is faulty, stop using it, tag it 'Out of service – do not use', and report it. Never try to repair electrical faults yourself unless you are qualified.

Key points

  • Choose the right tool and accessory for the job and material.
  • Never fit a disc rated lower than the tool's speed.
  • Inspect tools and accessories before use; wear eye, ear and face protection.
  • Clamp the work, use both hands and keep guards in place.
  • Disconnect power before changing accessories or cleaning.
  • Tag and report faulty tools; never use them.
